screens.title: Advanced Firewall Management with nftables
screens.subtitle: Modern packet filtering, sets, maps, and NAT for secure Linux systems

narration.text: In this lesson we'll move beyond iptables and learn nftables as the unified, modern firewall framework in the Linux kernel. You'll see why nftables matters: one tool and one syntax for IPv4, IPv6, ARP and bridging, improved performance via compact rule evaluation, and powerful data structures like sets and maps that let you group addresses and actions efficiently. We'll build a working ruleset that allows SSH, HTTP and HTTPS while dropping everything else, then extend it with NAT for port forwarding and masquerade for internal clients. You will also learn practical safeguards: loading the ruleset, making it persistent, and common troubleshooting checks so you don't lock yourself out. The lab included walks through creating an inet filter table, adding input, forward, and output chains, and configuring an ip nat table with prerouting and postrouting rules. By the end you'll be able to design a ruleset, translate policies into nft syntax, and debug rule order and connection tracking issues. Keep in mind a key habit: always allow established, related traffic before strict drops. That single rule prevents many accidental outages. Ready to explore real configurations and verification steps?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: nftables replaces iptables with a unified syntax and efficient data structures—use tables, chains, and rules plus sets/maps to write compact, high-performance firewall policies and NAT.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Advanced nftables

Advanced Firewall Management with nftables

Learn the nftables architecture, write compact rulesets with sets and maps, and configure NAT to safely forward and masquerade traffic for internal clients.

In this lesson
Architecture, rules, sets/maps, NAT, troubleshooting and a 15-minute lab-style walkthrough.
Why it matters
Unified, expressive rules simplify multi-protocol firewalls and improve performance in mixed IPv4/IPv6 environments.
Explore Key Topics
Three focused areas we'll cover in this chapter.
Tables & Chains
Sets & Maps
NAT & Forwarding
Concept map
table inet → chains (input, forward, output)
sets / maps → group addresses, map ports to verdicts

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: These objectives map to practical skills you must demonstrate. First, you will understand the nftables architecture and why it replaces iptables: one tool for multiple families, unified syntax, and a performance-focused evaluation model. Second, you'll be able to write and load nftables configuration: create tables, chains and rules for common services and apply them persistently. Third, you'll use advanced data structures—sets, maps and anonymous sets—to simplify rules and improve match performance when grouping addresses or mapping ports to actions. Fourth, you'll configure NAT and port forwarding with prerouting and postrouting chains so internal clients can access the internet and external clients can reach internal servers. Each objective includes short examples and a verification step, so you can demonstrate competency by loading a ruleset, testing SSH and HTTP access, and observing packet matches with nft monitor. These are practical, testable skills that matter during system hardening and network design.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practical Skills
screens.subtitle: How you will prove competence during the lab

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on verification and safety practices you'll adopt during hands-on work. First, always test rules with a permissive policy before switching to drop; this reduces the risk of accidental lockout. Second, include connection tracking early in your input chain with established and related states so responses to outgoing requests are allowed. Third, practice safe reloads: use nft -f to load configurations and nft list ruleset to inspect active rules. Fourth, debug with nft monitor and system logs to watch rule matches and service load errors. An important example: when you implement DNAT for port 8080 to an internal server, verify both the prerouting translation and that postrouting masquerade allows replies out to the internet. These verification skills are often the difference between a working firewall and one that breaks services. They will be assessed by testing SSH access, DNAT reachability, and internal client internet connectivity.

screens.title: Why nftables replaces iptables
screens.subtitle: Unified syntax, single utility, and efficient rule evaluation

narration.text: nftables changes how you think about packet filtering. Instead of separate tools and rule sets for IPv4, IPv6, ARP and bridging, nftables provides one command-line utility and a consistent syntax across protocol families. This reduces duplication and eliminates the need to maintain parallel configurations. Performance is improved because nftables evaluates rules via bytecode in the kernel and supports sets and maps for O(1)-like matching of large groups. A concrete example: when you group a dozen SSH client IPs into a named set, one rule can match them all rather than dozens of individual rules. A common misconception is assuming nftables simply renames iptables; it actually introduces new data structures and a different workflow, so copying iptables scripts verbatim may miss opportunities for simplification. To verify understanding, translate an iptables policy that allows SSH and HTTP into a compact nftables table using an inet family and test it with nft -f and nft list ruleset. The core takeaway: use nftables to reduce duplication, centralize control across families, and leverage sets and maps for scalable match logic. How would you consolidate two separate IPv4 and IPv6 rule files into a single inet table?

keyIdea.title: Comparison takeaway
keyIdea.text: nftables unifies protocol families and adds data structures that let you write shorter, faster, and easier-to-manage firewall policies.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › nftables vs iptables
Key differences and benefits
  • Single utility and syntax for multiple families (use inet to cover IPv4 and IPv6).
  • Sets and maps replace long repetitive rule lists and improve match performance.
  • Kernel-level bytecode evaluation reduces rule processing overhead.
  • Unified ruleset management simplifies persistence and inspection.
Concrete example
Group SSH clients into a set instead of writing multiple allow rules; one membership check matches all clients.
Common misconception

Treating nftables as a drop-in for iptables misses its strengths. Look for opportunities to replace long rule lists with sets and maps for clarity and speed.

Check your understanding
  1. Identify two iptables files you would consolidate into one inet table.
  2. List three advantages of using sets instead of repeated rules.
Key Takeaway

Use nftables to centralize firewall logic across families and replace repetitive rules with sets and maps for better performance.

screens.title: Tables, Chains and Hooks
screens.subtitle: The building blocks of an nftables ruleset

narration.text: Understanding tables, chains and hooks is essential before writing rules. A table is a container that holds chains and is declared for a specific family like ip, ip6, inet, bridge or arp. Chains are sequences of rules attached to kernel hooks—input, forward, output, prerouting and postrouting—so packets are processed at the right point in the network stack. Each chain has a type and a default policy, such as filter with policy drop or accept. For example, an inet table commonly contains an input chain with type filter hook input priority 0 and a policy drop to reject unspecified incoming traffic. A common error is misusing a family: placing IPv6 logic into an ip table rather than inet, which means IPv6 packets are not matched. A useful analogy is thinking of a table as a folder, chains as files inside that folder, and hooks as the mailroom where messages arrive for processing. Practice by declaring a table inet filter and an input chain, then add rules to allow loopback, established connections, and service ports. How does choosing inet simplify dual-stack deployments?

keyIdea.title: Structural insight
keyIdea.text: Tables group chains by family; chains attach to kernel hooks and define how packets are processed and whether the default policy accepts or drops them.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Tables, Chains & Hooks
Term definitions
Table: a named container assigned to a family (ip, ip6, inet, bridge, arp).
Chain: an ordered list of rules with a hook and a default policy, e.g., input, forward, output.
Hook: a kernel attachment point that determines when the chain runs, such as prerouting or postrouting for NAT.
Analogy
Think of a table as a folder, chains as files inside it, and hooks as the places where mail arrives for processing.
Practical example

Declare an inet table with an input chain set to policy drop, then allow loopback and established connections before port rules so responses are preserved.

Common mistake

Using ip instead of inet when you need to match both IPv4 and IPv6 will leave one family unmanaged. Prefer inet for dual-stack rules.

Key Takeaway

Structure your rules with the right table family and place stateful allowances early to preserve expected traffic flow.

screens.title: Build a Minimal inet Filter Ruleset
screens.subtitle: A working /etc/nftables.conf that permits SSH and web traffic

narration.text: Let's walk through a minimal but practical ruleset that secures a host while permitting common services. The example uses an inet table so both IPv4 and IPv6 are covered. The ruleset begins with flush ruleset to remove previous rules, then defines table inet filter with three chains: input, forward and output. The input chain uses type filter hook input priority 0 and sets a policy drop to deny unspecified traffic. Critical rules include allowing loopback interface traffic, accepting connection-tracked established and related flows, and then permitting TCP ports 22, 80 and 443. The output chain typically accepts outgoing traffic, while forward remains drop unless the server routes packets. Save this file as /etc/nftables. conf and load it with sudo nft -f /etc/nftables. conf. A common pitfall is placing a drop rule before ct state accept; always allow established and related first so replies and existing sessions continue. Try loading the file and then run sudo nft list ruleset to confirm the active configuration. What will you check first if SSH fails after load? Build a Minimal inet Filter Ruleset means a concise inet table with early loopback and connection-tracking rules lets you permit services while keeping a drop policy for everything else.. In practical terms, a working /etc/nftables.conf that permits ssh and web traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Working ruleset
keyIdea.text: A concise inet table with early loopback and connection-tracking rules lets you permit services while keeping a drop policy for everything else.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Minimal inet ruleset
Example /etc/nftables.conf
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f

flush ruleset

# Define an 'inet' table (applies to both IPv4 and IPv6)
table inet filter {
    chain input {
        type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;

        # Allow loopback interface traffic
        iif "lo" accept

        # Allow established and related connections
        ct state {established, related} accept

        # Allow SSH (port 22)
        tcp dport 22 accept

        # Allow HTTP (port 80)
        tcp dport 80 accept

        # Allow HTTPS (port 443)
        tcp dport 443 accept
    }

    chain forward {
        type filter hook forward priority 0; policy drop;
    }

    chain output {
        type filter hook output priority 0; policy accept;
    }
}
Explanation and checks
  • flush ruleset clears previous rules—use carefully on production systems.
  • iif "lo" accept preserves local traffic and prevents self-lockout.
  • ct state {established, related} accept must appear early to allow replies.
  • tcp dport rules open specific services; with policy drop everything else is denied.
Concrete example

After loading, run sudo nft list ruleset and try ssh to confirm connectivity. If SSH fails, check if ct state is present and that the SSH rule exists before drop rules.

Key Takeaway

Compose rules with loopback and connection tracking first, then add port permits; use policy drop to close unspecified paths.

screens.title: Sets, Maps and Anonymous Sets
screens.subtitle: Efficient grouping and mapping for scalable rules

narration.text: Sets and maps are where nftables becomes expressive and efficient. A set groups values like IP addresses, ports, or interfaces so one membership test replaces many equivalent rules. For example, define a set called ssh_clients typed as ipv4_addr with flags constant and elements listing trusted addresses; then match tcp dport 22 ip saddr @ssh_clients accept. A map maps one value to another, such as mapping a service port to a verdict so a single rule can vmap port numbers to accept or reject actions. Anonymous sets let you specify inline groups directly inside a rule using syntax like tcp dport {22, 80, 443} accept, which is convenient for small lists. A common misconception is that sets are only cosmetic; in high-rule-count environments sets improve lookups and reduce kernel work. Test a set by adding addresses, reloading, and then attempting connections from included and excluded IPs to confirm membership behavior. How might you use maps to route different ports to different verdicts without repeating rules? Sets, Maps and Anonymous Sets means use sets and maps to replace repeated rules with compact, efficient lookups—this improves readability and runtime performance.. In practical terms, efficient grouping and mapping for scalable rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Data-structure benefit
keyIdea.text: Use sets and maps to replace repeated rules with compact, efficient lookups—this improves readability and runtime performance.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Sets & Maps
Set example
set ssh_clients {
  type ipv4_addr;
  flags constant;
  elements = { 192.168.1.10, 192.168.1.20 }
}

# usage inside a chain
tcp dport 22 ip saddr @ssh_clients accept
This defines a named set you can reference by @ssh_clients, reducing repeated per-IP rules.
Map and anonymous set
map port_actions {
  type inet_service : verdict;
  elements = {
    22 : accept,
    80 : accept,
    443 : accept
  }
}

# anonymous set example
tcp dport { 22, 80, 443 } accept
Maps let you associate a key to an action so one rule can vmap ports to verdicts. Anonymous sets are quick inline lists for small groups.
Key Takeaway

Choose named sets for reuse and maps for key→action relationships; use anonymous sets for concise inline rules.

screens.title: Using vmap and Anonymous Sets
screens.subtitle: Compact actions with maps and inline groups

narration.text: Here we focus on combining maps and anonymous sets in rules to avoid repetition. The provided map, port_actions, maps service ports to a verdict. In a chain you can write tcp dport vmap @port_actions so the kernel applies the mapped verdict for matching ports. This approach is useful when you want a single rule to accept a set of ports without writing separate accept rules for each. Anonymous sets are convenient when the list is small: tcp dport {22, 80, 443} accept expresses allowed service ports in one concise expression. A practical pitfall: when you use vmap, ensure the map's type matches the key type—inet_service maps naturally to port numbers. Test by creating a map with 22, 80, 443 accept and then attempt to access those ports from a client; non-listed ports should be denied by the chain policy. A closing question to consider: when traffic must trigger different verdicts for different ports, how does using a map simplify the ruleset maintenance? Using vmap and Anonymous Sets means vmap with maps centralizes port-to-verdict decisions, while anonymous sets provide quick inline lists for small groups of ports.. In practical terms, compact actions with maps and inline groups. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Action mapping
keyIdea.text: vmap with maps centralizes port-to-verdict decisions, while anonymous sets provide quick inline lists for small groups of ports.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Maps & Anonymous Sets
Map example (vmap usage)
map port_actions {
  type inet_service : verdict;
  elements = {
    22 : accept,
    80 : accept,
    443 : accept
  }
}

# inside chain
tcp dport vmap @port_actions
Once defined, vmap consults the map and executes the matching verdict for a given port, avoiding multiple rules.
Anonymous set example
# inline list
tcp dport { 22, 80, 443 } accept
Good for small, static lists. If you expand the list frequently, move it to a named set for easier updates.
Check

After loading a map, test access to included ports from a client and confirm excluded ports are dropped by policy.

screens.title: NAT with nftables
screens.subtitle: DNAT for port-forwarding and SNAT/masquerade for outbound traffic

narration.text: Network Address Translation is critical when a firewall acts as a gateway for internal hosts. nftables handles NAT in an ip family table. DNAT belongs in the prerouting chain where the destination address can be changed before routing decisions. For example, to forward incoming SSH on a public IP 203.0.113.10 to an internal host 192.168.1.100:22 you add iifname "eth0" tcp dport 22 dnat to 192.168.1.100:22 in prerouting. SNAT or masquerade occurs in postrouting after routing decisions; for an internal network 192.168.60.0/24 using external interface eth0 you can write oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.60.0/24 masquerade. A common trap is misunderstanding prerouting vs postrouting: prerouting changes destination so the kernel can route to an internal server, whereas postrouting changes source so the external world sees the firewall's IP. Verify NAT by accessing the internal server from outside via the firewall's public port and by confirming internal clients can reach the internet. What steps will you take to verify both DNAT and SNAT flows? NAT with nftables means use prerouting for dnat/port forwarding and postrouting for snat/masquerade; this order reflects when destination and source must be altered in packet processing.. In practical terms, dnat for port-forwarding and snat/masquerade for outbound traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: NAT principle
keyIdea.text: Use prerouting for DNAT/port forwarding and postrouting for SNAT/masquerade; this order reflects when destination and source must be altered in packet processing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › NAT with nftables
DNAT example (prerouting)
table ip nat {
  chain prerouting {
    type nat hook prerouting priority -100;
    iifname "eth0" tcp dport 22 dnat to 192.168.1.100:22
  }

  chain postrouting {
    type nat hook postrouting priority 100;
    oifname "eth0" ip saddr 192.168.60.0/24 masquerade
  }
}
Prerouting changes destination before routing; postrouting alters source after routing to allow reply packets to reach the internet.
Verification checklist
  • From outside, attempt to reach public IP on forwarded port and confirm internal server responds.
  • On internal client, ping or browse internet to ensure masquerade allows egress.
  • Use sudo nft monitor to observe translation events in real time.
Key Takeaway

Place DNAT in prerouting and SNAT/masquerade in postrouting; verify both translation directions during testing.

screens.title: Load, Persist and Inspect Rulesets
screens.subtitle: Commands and best-practice sequence for safe deployment

narration.text: Loading and persisting a ruleset requires caution. Start by writing /etc/nftables. conf with your desired tables, chains, and rules. To load immediately, run sudo nft -f /etc/nftables. conf which parses and applies the configuration. Make it persistent by enabling nftables. service with sudo systemctl enable --now nftables. To inspect what the kernel is actually executing use sudo nft list ruleset. For live troubleshooting and to observe packet matches, run sudo nft monitor which streams events. A safe deployment sequence is: keep an active root or console session, load the new rules with nft -f, verify SSH and expected services, and only then change policies from accept to drop if you began permissive. A common mistake is flushing ruleset in production without fallback—flush ruleset removes all rules and may immediately disrupt connectivity. Always check journalctl -u nftables for service loading errors after enabling the service. Which command will you use first to confirm the ruleset loaded correctly? Load, Persist and Inspect Rulesets means write, load with nft -f, inspect with nft list ruleset, monitor with nft monitor, and persist with systemctl—always test before tightening policies.. In practical terms, commands and best-practice sequence for safe deployment. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Deployment routine
keyIdea.text: Write, load with nft -f, inspect with nft list ruleset, monitor with nft monitor, and persist with systemctl—always test before tightening policies.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Load & inspect
Safe load sequence
  1. Save /etc/nftables.conf with desired rules.
  2. Run sudo nft -f /etc/nftables.conf to apply changes.
  3. Verify with sudo nft list ruleset.
  4. Monitor real-time events with sudo nft monitor.
  5. Persist with sudo systemctl enable --now nftables once verified.
Troubleshooting commands
sudo nft list ruleset — view active kernel ruleset.
sudo nft monitor — watch matches and events in real time.
journalctl -u nftables — review service load errors.
Common Mistake

Running flush ruleset without a fallback can remove all protections. Keep a recovery path and test incrementally.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Server and Client Setup
screens.subtitle: Step-by-step configuration for a firewall/router with NAT

narration.text: Follow this lab sequence to build and verify a firewall that routes for an internal client. First, enable IP forwarding on the firewall by creating /etc/sysctl. d/99-ip-forward. conf with net. ipv4. ip_forward = 1 and apply it with sudo sysctl -p. Assume eth0 is the external interface and eth1 the internal one with internal network 192.168.60.0/24. Create /etc/nftables. conf containing a table inet filter with input/forward/output chains (policy drop on input and forward), and a table ip nat with prerouting DNAT rules and postrouting masquerade. Example DNAT forwards public port 8080 to 192.168.60.100:80. Load the config with sudo nft -f and enable the service with sudo systemctl enable --now nftables. On the internal client, set gateway to 192.168.60.1 and run a simple web server on port 80. Verify externally that curl to firewall_public_ip:8080 returns the internal web page. Use nft monitor to observe translations and nft list ruleset to confirm configurations. A common issue is forgetting to allow forwarding from eth1 to eth0; include an explicit iifname "eth1" oifname "eth0" accept rule in the forward chain. What verification command will show live translation events?

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Enable IP forwarding, configure inet filter and ip nat tables, load rules, and verify DNAT and SNAT by testing external and internal connectivity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Lab walkthrough
Server setup checklist
  • Create /etc/sysctl.d/99-ip-forward.conf and set net.ipv4.ip_forward = 1, then sudo sysctl -p.
  • Assume eth0 = external, eth1 = internal (192.168.60.1).
  • Write /etc/nftables.conf with inet filter (policy drop) and ip nat tables.
  • Load with sudo nft -f and persist with sudo systemctl enable --now nftables.
Client and verification
Set internal client gateway to 192.168.60.1 and run a web server on port 80.
From outside, curl http://firewall_public_ip:8080 to test DNAT to 192.168.60.100:80.
From internal client, ping 8.8.8.8 or browse to verify SNAT/masquerade allows egress.
Use sudo nft monitor to watch translation events live.
Reminder

Add forward rule iifname "eth1" oifname "eth0" accept so internal to external forwarding is permitted before drop policy takes effect.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them
screens.subtitle: Order, policies, lockout, flush ruleset, and interface names

narration.text: Troubleshooting nftables often comes down to a few recurring errors. First, rule order matters: placing a drop before a service allow will block traffic. The fix is to reorder or place ct state and service accepts early. Second, default policy: switching to policy drop without testing can take services offline; start permissive and tighten after verification. Third, locking yourself out is common—always ensure SSH is allowed or keep console access. Fourth, flush ruleset clears all rules immediately; avoid running it on production without a recovery plan. Fifth, interface names matter—iifname and oifname must match the system's actual interface names or rules won't match. Use nft list ruleset to inspect active rules and journalctl -u nftables for load errors. Tools like nft monitor show packet events, helping you see which rule matched. For practice, create a misordered rule set, then apply fixes and verify recovery by re-establishing SSH and service access. Which log or command would you check first if ruleset failed to load? Common Mistakes and How to Fix Them means check rule order, default policies, connection-tracking placement, interface names, and service logs; use nft list ruleset and nft monitor to observe behavior.. In practical terms, order, policies, lockout, flush ruleset, and interface names. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Troubleshoot checklist
keyIdea.text: Check rule order, default policies, connection-tracking placement, interface names, and service logs; use nft list ruleset and nft monitor to observe behavior.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.6 › Troubleshooting
Mistake
Rule placed too early that drops traffic.
Fix: Reorder rules and place ct state and service allows before drop.
Mistake
Switching to policy drop without tests.
Fix: Start policy accept, test, then change to drop after verification.
Mistake
Flushing ruleset on production.
Fix: Avoid flush ruleset; if used, have console access and an immediate recovery plan.
Mistake
Wrong interface names in rules.
Fix: Verify with ip link and update iifname/oifname values accordingly.
Useful commands
sudo nft list ruleset, sudo nft monitor, journalctl -u nftables
Practice tip
Intentionally misorder a rule set, observe failure, and then fix it while documenting the recovery steps.

screens.title: Hands-on Challenge and Verification Steps
screens.subtitle: A short lab to demonstrate complete firewall and NAT configuration

narration.text: This assessment challenge asks you to configure a firewall/router as described in the chapter and demonstrate three verifications. Task one: create an inet filter table with input policy drop that allows loopback, ct state established related, SSH, HTTP and HTTPS. Task two: create an ip nat table that DNATs public port 8080 to the internal web server at 192.168.60.100:80 and postrouting masquerades the internal network 192.168.60.0/24 on eth0. Task three: enable nftables service and show the ruleset with sudo nft list ruleset, then run tests: SSH to the firewall's public IP, curl the public IP:8080 from an external client to reach the internal web server, and from the internal client browse out to confirm SNAT works. A common verification misstep is forgetting the forward rule to allow eth1 to eth0 traffic; include iifname "eth1" oifname "eth0" accept. narration.text: As you finish this chapter, remember three practical reminders. First, always include ct state {established, related} early to avoid blocking replies and established sessions.
